paragraphs: Answering a question about a time series requires deciding where the relevant evidence lies. Some questions need the full sequence, while others depend on brief events or several separated intervals. ARTIST addresses this selection problem directly, instead of requiring every question to use a fixed representation of the entire series.

The method alternates between choosing temporal segments and reasoning about their contents. A controller selects informative intervals, and a reasoner uses those intervals to develop reasoning traces and answers. Reinforcement learning trains both roles, with a hierarchical policy optimization procedure coordinating segment selection and question answering. This makes information gathering part of the reasoning process itself.

Across six benchmarks, ARTIST improves average accuracy by 6.46 absolute percentage points over the strongest baseline. Its largest gains concern rare-event localization and reasoning across multiple segments. Supervised fine-tuning helps, while reinforcement learning adds further improvements through question-dependent selection. These findings support the value of learning what to inspect alongside learning how to answer.
icml-2026-adaptive-time-series-reasoning.tldr: ARTIST improves time-series question answering by learning to select relevant intervals as it reasons.

paragraphs: When training data contains many common examples and relatively few rare ones, fine-tuning a large vision-language model can reinforce the imbalance. The paper identifies early overfitting to frequent data as a problem: it interferes with learning rare cases while also failing to make full use of the abundant examples.

Adaptive Token Refinement addresses this through two operations at the token level. On the output side, a bounded adaptive loss dynamically filters and reweights tokens to reduce overfitting to frequent data. On the input side, a visual token masking strategy augments the probability paths available during learning. Together, these operations adjust both the supervision the model receives and the visual input it learns from.

The motivation also reflects a practical constraint: downstream datasets often lack quantified information about their imbalance, limiting methods that depend on such prior knowledge. Experiments report consistent improvements in performance and generalization for long-tailed fine-tuning. The contribution is an adaptive training framework aimed at improving learning across the imbalance, including the poorly served rare examples.
icml-2026-adaptive-token-refinement-in-l.tldr: Adaptive Token Refinement adjusts output-token learning and visual inputs to improve vision-language fine-tuning on imbalanced data.

paragraphs: Cybersecurity defenders need to connect multiple analytical tasks when investigating threats, from identifying their origins to responding to incidents. CYBERTEAM examines how language models perform this work when given a standardized workflow. Its focus is the organization of threat-hunting reasoning and the dependencies that determine which operations should happen first.

The benchmark builds this structure in two stages. It first represents dependencies among realistic analytical tasks, then assigns operational modules suited to each task's requirements. Models follow a sequence of reasoning steps grounded in discrete operations. In total, CYBERTEAM contains 30 tasks and nine modules, providing a common framework for guiding and assessing threat analysis.

The authors evaluate leading language models and cybersecurity agents, comparing the structured approach with open-ended reasoning strategies. They report improvements from standardization and identify limitations in open-ended reasoning for realistic threat hunting. The findings suggest that organizing a model's work around operational requirements and task dependencies can improve its usefulness in defensive analysis.
icml-2026-benchmarking-llm-assisted-blue.tldr: CYBERTEAM improves evaluation and guidance of defensive threat hunting through standardized tasks, operational modules, and reasoning dependencies.

paragraphs: A language model's confidence can remain poorly aligned with its accuracy after instruction tuning and preference alignment. CORAL addresses this at inference time, avoiding the expense of retraining the underlying model. Its central idea is to steer using signals directly related to correctness, rather than optimizing an indirect substitute.

CORAL uses small multilayer neural probes with weight-decay regularization to extract correctness information distributed across internal activations. Those signals guide inference-time steering. The emphasis on distributed information matters because a useful indication of correctness may be spread across the model's internal state, beyond what individual neurons can reveal.

Across three models with seven billion parameters, the authors report average accuracy improvements of 10% and expected calibration error improvements of 50%. Transfer to four held-out multiple-choice benchmarks without retraining yields average improvements of 14% and 49%, respectively. These results support the hypothesis that regularized probes can recover transferable correctness signals, with benefits for both answering accurately and expressing appropriately calibrated confidence.
icml-2026-correctness-optimized-residual.tldr: CORAL uses regularized probes of internal activations to improve multiple-choice accuracy and confidence calibration during inference.

paragraphs: Agents that operate graphical interfaces struggle to retain useful experience across long tasks spanning several applications. Simply accumulating memories introduces its own problems: high-level plans may not match execution details, and outdated experiences can contaminate the context. Darwinian Memory System treats memory as something that must be continually reorganized and selected.

The system breaks complex interaction histories into independent, reusable units that can be recombined. It then tracks their utility, removes less useful paths, and discourages high-risk plans. This selection process is intended to favor better strategies over time. Adaptation occurs through the contents and management of memory, without requiring model training or architectural additions.

On real-world benchmarks involving multiple applications, the authors report average gains of 18.0% in success rate and 33.9% in execution stability, alongside lower task latency. These findings indicate that memory quality and continued maintenance can materially affect an agent's behavior. The contribution combines reusable experience units with active removal of experiences that no longer help.
icml-2026-darwinian-memory-a-training-fr.tldr: Darwinian Memory improves GUI agents by retaining useful reusable experiences and pruning unhelpful or risky plans without model training.

paragraphs: A humanoid controller can imitate a motion poorly because its policy is inadequate or because the motion is intrinsically difficult to learn. Conventional error measurements describe the mismatch without separating these causes. The Torque Variation Score addresses that diagnostic gap by measuring motion difficulty independently of a particular policy's performance.

The score measures how much corrective torque must vary when a pose undergoes small perturbations. This connects difficulty to the motion's physical dynamics. The authors establish that high torque-variation motions produce flat reward landscapes and vanishing policy gradients, explaining why reinforcement learning can struggle to improve imitation even when errors persist.

Experiments with UHC and PHC+ find a strong relationship between the score and imitation error. High error on an easy motion points toward policy deficiency, while high error on a difficult motion reflects intrinsic learning constraints. The paper also develops capability assessment, difficulty-stratified error profiling, and detection of unusually difficult motion segments. These applications turn a difficulty measure into a tool for evaluating controllers and curating motion data.
icml-2026-distinguishing-imitation-error.tldr: The Torque Variation Score helps distinguish weak humanoid imitation policies from motions whose dynamics make learning intrinsically difficult.

paragraphs: Predicting a battery's lifetime early requires detecting degradation signals that are barely distinguishable from random fluctuations. Denoising or decomposing measurements can remove useful cues along with noise. DITING instead seeks to make weak degradation more distinguishable through a coupled comparison process inspired by the reliability benefits of two-sided hearing.

The method first uses selective matching based on optimal transport to build a robust health template from initial battery cycles. It then applies a tri-coupled mechanism designed to separate random fluctuations from accumulating degradation. Under symmetric coupling, matched responses suppress stochastic variation, while degradation-related deviations propagate into stable differences between the two sides.

This gives the method a way to amplify weak evidence through how responses differ, rather than relying solely on cleaning individual signals. Experiments across several datasets report state-of-the-art prediction performance and more reliable early support for battery lifecycle management. The stated findings connect better early prediction to a mechanism that preserves and strengthens subtle degradation cues.
icml-2026-diting-a-weak-degradation-list.tldr: DITING amplifies weak early battery degradation signals through coupled comparisons to improve lifetime prediction.

paragraphs: Language models can memorize sensitive or copyrighted training material, creating a need to suppress specific learned information. Existing unlearning methods can damage general usefulness or struggle with complex queries. Divergence Decoding approaches this problem by changing the model's output behavior during inference using smaller auxiliary models.

These auxiliary models steer the main model's logits, the scores underlying its output probabilities, away from targeted data. They are trained using standard pretraining and fine-tuning procedures. This places the initial intervention in the generation process. The authors also demonstrate that the resulting steered distribution can be distilled back into the base model.

Across unlearning benchmarks involving different model and dataset scales, Divergence Decoding decisively outperforms the stated leading baselines. The authors interpret this as evidence for an effective, inexpensive approach. They also explore image generation because the mechanism is generally applicable to probabilistic models, finding evidence of transfer beyond text. That image result supports broader applicability without establishing effectiveness in every probabilistic modeling domain.
icml-2026-divergence-decoding-inference-.tldr: Divergence Decoding uses small auxiliary models to steer generation away from targeted data and can distill that behavior into the base model.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts language models require substantial memory to store their expert networks. Compressing every expert equally overlooks differences in how often experts are used and how much information their weights contain. RFID-MoE uses both properties to decide where a limited compression budget should preserve more capacity.

The framework combines activation frequency with effective rank into an importance measure. It assigns higher approximation ranks to critical expert groups under a fixed budget. It also reconstructs information left out by compression through a sparse projection mechanism with few additional parameters. Thus, it addresses both allocation of retained capacity and recovery of discarded information.

Experiments across several compression ratios on models including Qwen3 and DeepSeekMoE report consistent improvements over MoBE and D²-MoE. For Qwen3-30B at a 60% compression ratio, the reported PTB perplexity is 16.92, more than 8.0 lower than the baselines; HellaSwag zero-shot accuracy improves by approximately 8%. These findings support accounting for unequal expert usage and information density when compressing MoE models.
icml-2026-effective-moe-based-llm-compre.tldr: RFID-MoE improves expert-model compression by allocating capacity according to expert usage and information density while recovering residual information.

paragraphs: Networks built from repeated blocks often develop structured relationships between layers during training. This paper asks whether optimization can benefit from those relationships. Its broader framework allows the update for one layer to depend on optimizer updates computed for other layers, making coordination across network depth an explicit part of training.

Gradient Smoothing implements this idea by applying structured smoothing operations to block-level update vectors. One example is a weighted average of nearby layers' updates. It works with updates from optimizers such as SGD, Adam, and Muon, with minimal computational overhead. The method also has a preconditioning interpretation: it transforms the proposed updates before they are applied.

Evaluations span language-model pretraining, reinforcement-learning post-training for reasoning, diffusion modeling, and vision-transformer classification. The authors report consistent improvements in convergence and generalization without changing architectures or objectives. They also observe more structured evolution of representations across depth. This suggests a connection between coordinated updates and internal representation organization, while leaving that connection as an interpretation of the evidence.
icml-2026-gradient-smoothing-coupling-la.tldr: Gradient Smoothing coordinates optimizer updates across layers to improve training convergence and generalization with little extra computation.

paragraphs: Masked diffusion models can be limited by sampling procedures that make earlier decisions irreversible. This becomes especially troublesome when generation must finish in only a few steps. The paper introduces a sampling method that gives pretrained models a way to revisit likely mistakes and improve the evolving output.

The approach reorganizes generation into a star-shaped process that permits error correction. A learned remasking module identifies decisions that may be wrong and marks them for revision. Adapting the pretrained model requires lightweight fine-tuning of a single layer. The central change therefore concerns how generation proceeds and how opportunities for correction are selected.

Experiments on text and code generation show that the method matches or outperforms existing approaches. The authors report particularly substantial quality gains when using few sampling steps, alongside improvements in efficiency. Component ablations and tests in different scenarios examine the contribution and usability of the design. The results indicate that selective revision can make limited-step masked diffusion generation more effective.
icml-2026-guided-star-shaped-masked-diff.tldr: A star-shaped sampling process and learned remasking let masked diffusion models correct mistakes, especially when generation uses few steps.

paragraphs: This paper studies the range of sequences a transformer can produce from prompts, asking how much that range can be predicted from a few architectural characteristics. It defines an accessible sequence as one the transformer can output for some prompt and develops a prompt-length-dependent upper bound on the number of distinct outputs.

The theoretical results connect prompt length to several restrictions. The maximum accessible sequence length grows linearly with prompt length, and the coefficient in that relationship has a theoretical upper bound. Beyond a critical threshold, the fraction of sequences that are accessible shrinks exponentially as sequence length increases. The stated results continue to hold with unbounded context and computation time.

Empirical tests across architectures and model sizes find the output-count bound tight within a factor smaller than ten. The analysis also explains previously observed failures on copying and cramming tasks. Together, these findings connect architectural constraints to output diversity and sequence-task behavior, showing that additional context and computation alone do not remove the restrictions established by the analysis.
icml-2026-how-many-different-outputs-can.tldr: The paper derives architectural bounds linking prompt length to the number and length of sequences a transformer can output.

paragraphs: Cooperative agents can fail as a team when individual members malfunction. MARTA trains for this problem by introducing faults selectively at states where they strongly affect performance. It adds a robustness mechanism to existing multi-agent reinforcement-learning algorithms without requiring changes to their architectures.

The mechanism separates two decisions. A Switcher chooses when a fault occurs and which agent fails; an Adversary determines the faulty behavior through random or worst-case policies. This creates a Markov game with two additional players. The authors develop a Q-learning-style scheme and establish contraction of its Bellman operator, supporting a unique minimax value and convergence to a Markov perfect equilibrium.

Evaluations cover Traffic Junction, Level-Based Foraging, MPE SimpleTag, and SMAC. Reported final-performance gains reach 116.7% in SMAC, 21.4% in SimpleTag, and 44.6% in Foraging. Failure rates also decline when test faults differ from training faults. These results support targeted fault induction as a way to strengthen cooperative policies against malfunction patterns beyond those encountered during training.
icml-2026-learning-robust-multi-agent-po.tldr: MARTA improves cooperative-agent robustness by learning when to induce malfunctions and how faulty agents should behave during training.

paragraphs: Removing semantic image watermarks involves competing goals: suppressing detection, preserving appearance, and keeping computation low. The paper argues that current approaches do not achieve all three simultaneously. DAWN targets the inexpensive end of this trade-off, offering a training-free method with competitive removal performance and modest perceptual degradation.

The method uses natural-image priors in two complementary spaces: frequency and semantic representations. It projects the image toward those priors to suppress watermark signals that depart from natural statistics. A separate perceptual-alignment stage then restores visual consistency. Separating suppression from alignment allows the design to address both detectability and the visual artifacts introduced during removal.

Across watermarking schemes operating in pixel, frequency, and latent spaces, the authors report consistent reductions in detectability while retaining structural and semantic fidelity. These findings show that low-resource removal can be feasible without the expensive multistep optimization associated with existing attacks. The reported outcome remains a trade-off: computational savings and removal effectiveness come with some perceptual degradation.
icml-2026-low-compute-watermark-removal-.tldr: DAWN reduces image-watermark detectability using inexpensive natural-image projections while accepting modest perceptual degradation.

paragraphs: Strong chess performance on familiar positions does not by itself establish systematic understanding of rules or strategy. This paper examines a 270-million-parameter transformer trained by behavior cloning on standard chess. The authors construct unfamiliar board configurations and chess variants to test how its behavior extends beyond its training distribution.

The evaluation separates legal play from strategic quality. The model consistently produces legal moves in novel configurations, providing evidence of robust rule-based reasoning. It also finds high-quality moves on curated unfamiliar puzzles and shows basic strategic adaptation in complete games. However, its strategic reasoning is more limited than its ability to respect the rules.

Explicit-search symbolic algorithms outperform the transformer, although the gap is smaller when playing against human users on Lichess. Analysis of training reveals distinct phases in learning the game's fundamental constraints, suggesting an emerging compositional understanding. The contribution is a differentiated account of generalization: rule following transfers strongly in these tests, while strategic decision-making presents a more uneven picture.
icml-2026-out-of-distribution-evaluation.tldr: An unfamiliar-position evaluation finds strong rule generalization in a chess transformer but more limited strategic reasoning.

paragraphs: Estimating causal effects with hidden confounders motivates instrumental-variable regression. One established approach learns spectral features from the mathematical operator relating treatments to instruments. These features capture its dominant singular subspaces, but their construction ignores the outcome being predicted. Consequently, they can represent the true causal function poorly.

Augmented Spectral Feature Learning makes this representation step sensitive to the outcome. The authors construct an augmented operator that includes outcome information and derive a contrastive loss from it. Minimizing that loss produces features tailored to the causal estimation task, addressing the mismatch between dominant treatment–instrument structure and the function of interest.

The paper provides theoretical analysis and evaluates the framework on challenging benchmarks. Its stated finding is that outcome-aware features remain effective under spectral misalignment, the situation in which conventional dominant features miss relevant causal structure. The broader significance is that feature selection for instrumental-variable estimation can benefit from considering the outcome during representation learning, alongside the relationship between treatments and instruments.
icml-2026-outcome-aware-spectral-feature.tldr: Outcome-aware spectral features improve instrumental-variable regression when conventional features poorly represent the causal function.

paragraphs: Estimating differential entropy is difficult when a distribution is known only up to an unknown normalization constant. Particle-based variational methods offer a possible route, but the paper identifies obstacles in P-SVGD that prevent scaling to high dimensions. These include incorrect invertibility assumptions, a missing trace-of-Hessian term, and unstable divergence-control heuristics.

MET-SVGD extends that method with a framework for stable hyperparameter selection and guarantees of global invertibility and convergence. These properties address the mathematical and numerical weaknesses identified in the earlier approach. The aim is to make entropy estimation workable as dimensionality increases while retaining a principled treatment of the particle transformations.

Experiments report up to 12-fold lower entropy-estimation error than P-SVGD and 16-fold lower error than existing SVGD baselines. On CIFAR-10 energy-based generation, the method improves FID by 80.4% and reports 64-fold higher training stability. Maximum-entropy reinforcement learning yields up to 16% higher returns than P-SVGD. These results connect the methodological repairs to benefits in both estimation and downstream learning.
icml-2026-particles-dont-care-about-z-to.tldr: MET-SVGD repairs theoretical and stability problems in particle-based entropy estimation and improves reported estimation and downstream results.

paragraphs: Neural vehicle-routing solvers must search large spaces of possible routes while accommodating different task constraints. Their performance can be limited by weak representations, unstable training, and inefficient exploration. PoMtVRS addresses these issues through a framework that combines changes to decoder representations with an objective based on preferences among candidate solutions.

The preference objective teaches the solver relative comparisons between routes across different tasks, increasing the generation probability of better solutions. A preference-gated block also adapts the decoder's representations using sparse gated attention and nonlinear residual refinement. These components work together: one improves how the decoder represents its decisions, while the other directs learning toward more desirable outcomes.

The framework is designed to attach to existing unified neural routing backbones. Extensive experiments report improvements to state-of-the-art backbones, leading performance on multi-task benchmarks, and stronger generalization. The findings support combining representation refinement with preference-driven optimization to improve a solver's use of its search space across routing tasks.
icml-2026-pomtvrs-preference-optimized-m.tldr: PoMtVRS improves multi-task vehicle routing by combining preference-based solution learning with adaptive decoder refinement.

paragraphs: Numerical solvers for partial differential equations often use operator splitting to organize a problem into component operations. Learning-based hybrid solvers can improve classical methods, but their architectures are frequently designed without an explicit connection to that underlying structure. This paper develops a framework that makes the connection systematic.

The authors show how an operator splitting scheme naturally determines an unrolled architecture, where algorithmic steps become the structure of the model. Within this framework, a broad range of existing plug-and-play and hybrid models appear as special cases. This gives different designs a common mathematical description and provides a route from optimization algorithms to new architectures.

Using that route, the paper introduces new unrolled hybrid models and evaluates them on benchmark fluid-dynamics simulations. The reported models improve both accuracy and stability. The significance is therefore both conceptual and practical: the framework explains relationships among existing architectures and uses the same structural connection to guide designs that perform better in the tested simulations.
icml-2026-proximal-splitting-methods-for.tldr: The paper derives hybrid learning architectures from operator splitting schemes and reports improved fluid-simulation accuracy and stability.

paragraphs: Assessing video quality requires sensitivity to distortion and motion as well as semantic content. The paper argues that transferring semantic knowledge from large classification datasets is insufficient, while the pretraining itself can be expensive. Q-CLIP builds video quality assessment around pretrained contrastive vision-language models and a small adaptation mechanism.

A shared cross-modal adapter improves both visual and textual representations. It contains few trainable parameters and is described as the only component requiring training, substantially reducing computational cost. The framework also introduces five learnable quality-level prompts to help distinguish subtle differences in quality. The authors additionally investigate how choosing different video frames affects assessment.

Experiments report strong performance on several video-quality datasets. The approach matters because it connects efficient adaptation with the need to represent quality through both visual and textual information. Its stated results support using a compact shared adapter to draw more useful quality judgments from existing vision-language representations, while the frame-sampling investigation addresses another consequential part of the assessment pipeline.
icml-2026-q-clip-unleashing-the-power-of.tldr: Q-CLIP uses a small shared visual-textual adapter and quality-level prompts for efficient video quality assessment.

paragraphs: Bayesian posterior sampling can become computationally practical by estimating gradients from minibatches, but the resulting noise can make sampling unstable. Stochastic Gradient Lattice Random Walk addresses sensitivity to minibatch size and gradient noise through a different discretization of the sampling process. It extends an existing lattice random-walk approach.

The distinguishing feature is how stochastic noise enters the update covariance: SGLRW introduces it only through off-diagonal elements. The authors connect this design to greater robustness across minibatch sizes while retaining asymptotic correctness. They also analyze a gradient-clipped analogue of Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics as a comparison, examining another way to handle troublesome gradients.

Experiments on Bayesian regression and classification find that SGLRW stays stable in settings where SGLD fails, including settings with heavy-tailed gradient noise. Predictive performance matches or improves on the comparison method. The findings indicate that changing the structure of the sampling update can improve practical robustness while preserving the method's stated long-run correctness property.
icml-2026-robust-stochastic-gradient-pos.tldr: SGLRW changes the covariance structure of stochastic-gradient sampling to improve robustness while retaining asymptotic correctness.

paragraphs: Local small language models can handle relatively simple requests, while more capable remote models introduce monetary costs. Selective Deferred Routing seeks a better balance by letting the local model attempt a request before deciding whether remote assistance is worthwhile. That initial attempt also provides information for the routing decision.

The local model produces a preliminary answer and rich semantic representations of the request. A lightweight decision module uses this information to choose between accepting the local answer and sending the request to a suitable remote model. The decision therefore benefits from work already performed on the request, including the model's generated response.

Experiments cover multiple model architectures and families, along with datasets spanning several task scenarios. The method consistently outperforms existing multi-model collaboration approaches across a broad range of cost–performance trade-offs. These findings support deferring routing until after local processing: the local attempt serves both as a possible final response and as evidence for choosing a stronger model when needed.
icml-2026-selective-deferred-routing-ena.tldr: Selective Deferred Routing uses a local model's initial work to decide whether to accept its answer or pay for a suitable remote model.

paragraphs: Language-model agents often solve recurring situations from scratch, repeating computation and introducing inconsistent behavior. Skill-Pro turns interaction experience into reusable procedural knowledge without updating model parameters. Its aim is to make past experience directly executable, so that an agent can reuse a procedure instead of repeatedly deriving it.

The framework defines a Skill-MDP and represents each skill through activation, execution, and termination conditions. These specify when a procedure applies, what it does, and when it ends. A Non-Parametric PPO process uses semantic gradients to generate candidates and a PPO Gate to verify them. Score-based maintenance then keeps the procedural memory compact and focused on useful skills.

Experiments examine reuse within a domain, across tasks, and across agents. The authors report superior reuse rates and significant gains together with extreme memory compression. Visualizations show skills accumulating, being refined, and being reused over time. The contribution combines executable skill definitions, candidate verification, and memory maintenance into an inspectable process for learning from experience.
icml-2026-skill-pro-learning-reusable-sk.tldr: Skill-Pro converts agent experience into verified reusable procedures and maintains them in compact memory without parameter updates.

paragraphs: Digital-health systems need useful clinical reasoning together with reliability and manageable deployment costs. This paper questions whether increasing the size of a single language model is the best way to meet those needs. It studies Small Agent Groups, motivated by the collaborative nature of clinical decision-making.

The group distributes reasoning, evidence-based analysis, and critical auditing across a deliberative process. This organization gives collaboration a central role in producing and scrutinizing clinical judgments. The evaluation considers effectiveness, reliability, and deployment cost, allowing the proposed approach to be assessed across several dimensions of clinical utility rather than a single performance measure.

The authors report that Small Agent Groups outperform a single giant model both with and without additional optimization or retrieval-augmented generation. They interpret these findings as evidence that collaborative reasoning can substitute for parameter growth in clinical settings. The results support this alternative within the evaluated configurations and suggest that coordinating smaller agents can offer a better balance of capability, reliability, and deployment efficiency.
icml-2026-small-agent-group-is-the-futur.tldr: Small Agent Groups distribute clinical reasoning and auditing, outperforming a single giant model in the paper's evaluations.

paragraphs: Linear recurrent neural networks are attractive language-model architectures partly because their computations can be parallelized efficiently. This paper explains why linear recurrence has that advantage over traditional nonlinear recurrence by connecting network types to computational complexity classes. The analysis treats parallelizability as a property of the computations each architecture can express.

The authors represent linear RNNs as bounded-fan-in arithmetic circuits with logarithmic depth, placing them close to the logarithmic-depth Boolean circuits associated with transformers. Nonlinear RNNs can solve L-complete problems and, with polynomial precision, even P-complete problems. These results expose a fundamental complexity-theoretic barrier to making nonlinear recurrence as parallelizable as transformers.

The analysis also distinguishes linear variants: permutation-diagonal models are NC¹-complete, while diagonal-plus-low-rank models have the greater expressivity characterized by PNC¹-completeness. Corresponding automata models provide another account of what each architecture can simulate. Together, the results explain why recurrence alone does not determine parallel efficiency and give architecture designers a theoretical basis for weighing expressive power against opportunities for parallel computation.
icml-2026-why-are-linear-rnns-more-paral.tldr: Complexity-theoretic connections explain linear RNNs' parallel efficiency and distinguish the expressive power of recurrent architectures.
